name: Vädda language, 'VL'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Geiger, Wilhelm. 1935. The Language of the Väddās. The Indian Historical Quarterly 11: 504-516 (Calcutta, ed. N. N. Law).
catalog_quote: The vowel a, apparently pronounced as indifferent vowel ə after the accentuated syllable, is frequently written e: mangacenawa, to go, S. 437, No. 88 ... As to pronunciation we must keep in mind that the accent generally lies on the first syllable of the word and that the vowel a after the accent is = ə (i.e. indifferent vowel). In compounds each word has its own accent.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened the page scan (printed p. 506 of Geiger 1935, 'The Language of the Väddās', IHQ 11: 504-516; p. 538 of the 915-page archive.org DLI scan). Both quoted passages are there verbatim: (i) para. 1: 'The vowel a, apparently pronounced as indifferent vowel ə after the accentuated syllable, is frequently written e: mangacenawa, to go, S. 437, No. 88..'; (ii) lower on the same page, prefacing the conversational sentences: 'As to pronunciation we must keep in mind that the accent generally lies on the first syllable of the word and that the vowel a after the accent is = ə (i.e. indifferent vowel). In compounds each word has its own accent.' the compilers ellipsis joins these two places on one…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent generally falls on the first syllable; post-accentual short a reduces to schwa; in compounds each member keeps its own (initial) accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; only that each member of a compound carries its own accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedged with 'generally'; Geiger also warns that in sung/recited texts vowel length is distorted by musical recitation (p. 505), so the remark is framed for conversational sentences.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level pronunciation note prefacing conversational sentences (Seligmann pp. 388-9 and Geiger's own 1896 Bintenne material); Geiger treats Vedda as a peculiar dialect of colloquial Sinhalese, whose accent he elsewhere (1938 grammar sec. 6) calls initial and 'rather a pitch than a stress'. Old (1935), philological, impressionistic; no modern instrumental or phonological treatment of Vedda stress was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Geiger 1935 describes the 'Vadda language (VL)' as a whole, drawing on published texts from Southern (Nilgala, Sita Vanniya), Northern (Bintenne) and Coast Veddas plus his own 1896 Bintenne material; the accent remark is given as a general pronunciation note for the conversational sentences (from Seligmann pp. 388-9 and his own Bintenne collection). Same languoid as vedd1240; note Geiger treats VL as a peculiar dialect of colloquial Sinhalese, and his initial-accent statement parallels his own description of Sinhalese (Geiger 1938 sec. 6: accent on first syllable, 'rather a pitch than a stress').
